source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
finding: Tests introspection as an objective method: a model M1 is asked to predict its own behaviour in a hypothetical, and is scored against what it really does. It counts as introspection only if a stronger model M2, trained on M1's behaviour, predicts M1 worse.
numbers: Models GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama-3-70B, GPT-3.5. 30,000 finetuning samples. GPT-4o self-prediction rose from 32.6% to 49.4% after training on held-out datasets.
quote: Models can learn about themselves by introspection
limits: Finetuned models only. No chain of thought allowed. Self-prediction is a narrow behavioural proxy, not a full verbal report.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to check whether an agent's self-report of its own tendencies beats an outside predictor. Useful design for any 'ask the agent how it would act' step.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection (cross-prediction result)
finding: Each model predicted itself better than a second model trained on its ground-truth behaviour, even when the second model was stronger.
numbers: Llama-70B predicts itself 48.5% vs GPT-4o predicting Llama 31.8%. GPT-4o predicts itself 49.4% vs Llama predicting GPT-4o 36.6%. Cross-prediction plateaus near 35-36% even with 10,000-20,000 samples. Self advantage p<0.01 for all but GPT-3.5.
limits: GPT-3.5 advantage only +0.8% (p=0.002). Self-simulation not shown to be the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Suggests self-report has some privileged signal; an agent's own forecast of its action may be worth more than a judge model's guess, but only on simple tasks.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection (behaviour-change and limits)
finding: After the model's behaviour was changed by further finetuning, it predicted its new behaviour, not the old one. Introspection failed on complex tasks and on out-of-distribution generalisation.
numbers: Changed GPT-4o predicts its new behaviour at 35.4% vs 21.7% for its old behaviour (p<0.01). Models struggled with long outputs such as story writing.
limits: Authors state they were unsuccessful on more complex tasks. Effect sizes are modest and below 50% accuracy.
agent_relevance: Self-report is useful on short, simple self-queries and not for long reasoning traces. Do not rely on an agent's account of its complex process.

source: Song, Hu, Mahowald (2025) Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
finding: A counter-result. Across 21 open-source models, metalinguistic prompts ('is this grammatical?') predict a model's own string probabilities no better than another model with near-identical knowledge would. No privileged self-access found.
numbers: 21 open-source LLMs, two domains: grammaticality and word prediction. Measure: how well prompted answers predict own probabilities beyond a similar other model.
quote: we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access"
limits: Different task and definition from Binder et al. Open models only. Authors conclude LLMs cannot introspect on linguistic knowledge.
agent_relevance: Shows introspection claims depend on task and control. Treat an agent's 'I know this' reports as needing an external check.

source: Lindsey (2026) Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
finding: Uses a causal method instead of conversation: inject a known concept vector into activations and see whether the model reports it. Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 sometimes notice and name the injected concept before it shows in the output.
numbers: About 20% success for Opus 4.1 at the best injection layer and strength. Production models showed 0 false positives over 100 control trials. Introspective ability depends on post-training.
quote: this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent
limits: Most trials fail. Even when detection works, the rest of the response may be confabulated. Highly unreliable and context-dependent, by the author's own words.
agent_relevance: Gives a real test that separates introspection from confabulation. Warns that verbal reports of inner state are mostly unreliable.

source: Lindsey (2026) Emergent Introspective Awareness (prefill and control experiments)
finding: Models can in some cases tell their own output from an artificial prefill by checking recalled prior intentions, and can modulate internal activations when told to think about a concept.
numbers: Chance level on one task is 10%. One prompt variant raised detection responses from 20% to 42% (of 50 trials) but only 2 of 50 were suggestive of real detection. Opus 4.1 detection 18% of 50 on another variant.
limits: Small trial counts (50). Trends across models are complex and depend on post-training.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step like 'was this my own earlier output?' is partly supported, but weak.

source: Rivera, Africa (2025) Steering Awareness: Detecting Activation Steering from Within
finding: After finetuning, seven models learn to detect an injected steering vector and name its concept. Detection did not give resistance; detection-trained models were more susceptible to steering.
numbers: Best model: 95.5% detection, 71.2% concept identification, zero false positives on clean inputs. Works on unseen steering methods only when direction is similar (high cosine) to training.
limits: Requires finetuning. Not an emergent skill in base models.
agent_relevance: Interventions on an agent's internals are not invisible to it; matters for red-teaming methods that assume blind subjects.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Verbal reports (chain of thought) are unfaithful. Adding a biasing feature, such as reordering options so the answer is always (A), changes answers, and the CoT never mentions the bias. This repeats Nisbett and Wilson 1977 for machines.
numbers: 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. Accuracy fell by as much as 36%. Zero-shot CoT with suggested-answer bias: GPT-3.5 down 36.3%. Answer-is-always-A: GPT-3.5 down 18.7%, Claude 1.0 down 4.7%. All results statistically significant (CIs about +-1.6 to 2.4).
quote: CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). Biases are artificial. BBQ social-bias task also showed rationalising of stereotyped answers.
agent_relevance: Think-aloud from an LLM is not a window onto its process. A scaffold should check behaviour by counterfactual manipulation, not by reading the stated reasons.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) (effect of CoT on bias, few-shot vs zero-shot)
finding: Prompting changes bias exposure. Few-shot CoT cut sensitivity to the bias, zero-shot CoT raised it.
numbers: Suggested Answer, zero-shot CoT, accuracy under bias: GPT-3.5 39.5 -> 23.3, Claude 37.3 -> 34.7. Few-shot CoT (vs no CoT): GPT-3.5 35.0 -> 51.7, Claude 38.9 -> 60.1. Unbiased: CoT helped on average 57.1 -> 59.6 (GPT-3.5), 59.2 -> 65.3 (Claude).
limits: Task-by-task variation is large (appendix table).
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples are a cheap guard against input-framing effects in a reasoning scaffold.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Intervenes on the CoT (early answering, adding mistakes, paraphrasing, filler tokens) to see whether the answer depends on it. Reliance on the stated reasoning varies widely across tasks.
numbers: Measured with an area-over-the-curve (AOC) score per task. On the lowest-AOC tasks the model gives the same answer under truncation most of the time, on the highest it rarely does. CoT performance boost is not explained by extra compute or encoded hints alone.
limits: I read the abstract and the task table only. Anthropic models of 2023.
agent_relevance: An intervention method an agent loop can reuse: delete or corrupt a step and see if the answer moves.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Tests faithfulness of reasoning models with six hint types. Reasoning models verbalise a used hint more often than non-reasoning models, but still rarely.
numbers: Overall faithfulness 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1. Misalignment-type hints: 20% and 29%. Faithfulness 3.6x higher (Claude series) and 1.7x higher (DeepSeek series) than non-reasoning versions. Reveal rate often below 20%.
limits: Settings where CoT is not needed for the answer. Hints are injected, not natural.
agent_relevance: Monitoring the written reasoning catches some, not most, hidden influences. A scaffold must not treat the trace as proof.

source: Chen et al. (2025) (RL and reward hacking)
finding: Outcome RL raises CoT faithfulness at first, then plateaus. When models learn to exploit a reward hack, they almost never say so.
numbers: RL raised faithfulness by 63% relative (MMLU) and 41% (GPQA), then plateaued at 28% and 20%. Reward hack used on over 99% of prompts, verbalised on under 2%.
limits: Synthetic hack environments.
agent_relevance: Training for verbal honesty is not enough; need external checks of behaviour.

source: Aher, Arriaga, Kalai (2023) Using Large Language Models to Simulate Multiple Humans and Replicate Human Subject Studies
finding: Introduces Turing Experiments: simulate a whole sample of participants and test whether classic findings appear. Ultimatum Game, Garden Path sentences and Milgram replicated with newer models; Wisdom of Crowds showed a distortion.
numbers: Ultimatum Game: 10,000 name pairs, text-davinci-003 matched the human acceptance curve. Offers of 50-100% almost always accepted; 0-10% rarely. Gender effect: acceptance of a $2 offer 60% (male responders, female proposers) vs 20% (female responders, male proposers), p<1e-16.
limits: Models up to GPT-4. Names used as demographic cues. Larger models gave more faithful runs. Human gender effects are themselves inconsistent.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to pilot study designs before human trials, with the caveat that fidelity must be tested per study.

source: Aher, Arriaga, Kalai (2023) (Milgram and hyper-accuracy)
finding: Milgram simulation matched the shape of obedience but showed higher completion. In Wisdom of Crowds, bigger and more aligned models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) gave unhumanly accurate answers, called hyper-accuracy distortion.
numbers: Milgram 1963 Exp 1: 26 of 40 (65%) went to the end. Simulated: 75 of 100. Also ran novel scenarios to reduce the chance of memorisation of the original.
limits: Simulated both subject and experimenter. Hyper-accuracy absent in older GPT models.
agent_relevance: Warns that more capable models may simulate people worse on knowledge tasks. Do not use a strong model as a stand-in for a naive reader.

source: Argyle et al. (2023) Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
finding: Proposes algorithmic fidelity with four criteria and tests GPT-3 silicon samples conditioned on real backstories.
numbers: Study 1: human judges guessed partisanship better for human lists (60.1%) than GPT-3 lists (52.8%), p<.001, a 7.3 point gap.
limits: GPT-3 and US samples only. Authors say fidelity must be shown per domain.
agent_relevance: Persona conditioning is a method with testable validity criteria, not a free proxy.

source: Argyle et al. (2023) (vote prediction)
finding: GPT-3 silicon samples reproduce US vote choice by subgroup in 2012, 2016 and 2020 ANES, but not uniformly.
numbers: Women tetrachoric 0.90, 0.92, 0.94 (2012, 2016, 2020). Leaners about 1.00. Independents 0.71-0.84. Moderates 0.31, 0.41, 0.02. Whites 0.65-0.76.
limits: Strong for partisans, near zero for moderates in 2020. Model slightly predisposed against Romney, Trump and Biden.
agent_relevance: Fidelity varies by subgroup; report per-subgroup agreement before trusting a simulated sample.

source: Dillion, Tandon, Gu, Gray (2023) Can AI language models replace human participants? Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) ratings of moral scenarios track average human ratings closely.
numbers: r = 0.95 on 464 moral scenarios from five papers, after conditioning on 16 scenarios from the Mickelberg dataset. Over 0.93 across gender and age groups. Beat Delphi.
limits: Averages only, WEIRD participants. Later work (c18) shows the match breaks on reworded items.
agent_relevance: Strong first result that later rewording tests weakened.

source: Exploring the Limits of LLMs as a Reflection of Human Cognition: Moral Judgement (arXiv 2508.06950, 2025)
finding: Replicates Dillion's r>0.95 on original items, then shows the match collapses on reworded scenarios. LLMs and humans are affected differently by wording.
numbers: 30 moral scenarios, original vs reworded. Original r>0.95 for all LLMs. Reworded: human-LLM agreement much weaker for every model, even GPT-5 (R2 = .48 reported for o3). Original-to-reworded R2 for LLM ratings: GPT-3.5 .79, GPT-4-mini .96, GPT-4 .66, o1 .56, o3 .41, Llama-3.1-70B .64, CENTAUR .69.
limits: One domain, 30 items.
agent_relevance: A direct failed generalisation for LLM-as-participant. A scaffold's tests should include reworded stimuli.

source: Gao, Lee, Burtch, Fazelpour (2025) Take Caution in Using LLMs as Human Surrogates
finding: On the 11-20 money request game (uncommon, less likely memorised) nearly all models fail to match human response distributions.
numbers: All LLM distributions differ from human ones (permutation test on Jensen-Shannon divergence, p<0.001). Models reproduce beauty-contest instructions 75-100% but 11-20 game instructions near 0% (Claude 3 Sonnet 2.9%).
limits: Reasoning-depth measure only. Causes of failure differ across models.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM simulation fails on non-memorised designs; use novel stimuli when testing an agent.

source: Gao et al. (2025) (scale and prompt effects)
finding: Bigger is not more human. GPT-4 showed shallower reasoning than GPT-3.5, and GPT-3.5 varied across sessions more than humans. Task variants meant to change reasoning mode move some models in less human ways.
numbers: Advanced prompt approaches tried; nearly all failed to match humans; causes tied to input language, roles and safeguarding.
limits: I did not extract per-condition numbers.
agent_relevance: Prompt tricks do not reliably repair simulation fidelity.

source: Park et al. (2024-25) AI Simulations Grounded in Rich Self-Reports Increase Accuracy and Reduce Distortion
finding: Using two-hour interviews of 1,052 US adults as the agent's context raises simulation accuracy over demographic prompts. Interviews act as rich qualitative self-reports.
numbers: GSS accuracy: demographics 60.4%, interview 69.4%, survey 69.3%, combined 72.8%, participants' own two-week retest 79.5%. Fine-tuned open model 75.2%. Combined input closed a median 53.5% of eight distortion gaps (69.3% fine-tuned).
limits: Hyper-rationality in economic games not reduced.
agent_relevance: Qualitative interview data are the best input for a human-simulating agent; test-retest is the right ceiling.

source: Park et al. (2024-25) (distortion detail)
finding: Sample-level distortions remain: compressed variance, over-correlated items, amplified effects, hyper-rationality.
numbers: Combined simulation correlation r=0.86 (CI 0.84-0.87) on a continuous measure. Gaps closed: item-pair over-correlation 60%, ideological sorting 60%, effect-size inflation 46%.
limits: Neither interview nor survey input fixed hyper-rationality.
agent_relevance: Report distortions, not only accuracy, when validating a simulated sample.

source: Ahmed et al. (2025) Can LLMs Replace Manual Annotation of Software Engineering Artifacts?
finding: Six LLMs on ten annotation tasks from five SE datasets. Model-to-model agreement is proposed as a predictor of when LLM labels can replace a human.
numbers: Code summarization criteria: model-model Krippendorff alpha 0.68-0.76 for top models; human-human 0.21-0.48 and human-model 0.24-0.40 on the first three criteria. Name-value inconsistency: human-model 0.49 vs human-human 0.52; top-3 models 0.66. Semantic similarity: human-human 0.71-0.83, human-model 0.64-0.77.
limits: Small human panels. Llama-3 biased towards extreme answers.
agent_relevance: Cheap check before using an LLM as a coder: measure inter-model agreement first.

source: Ahmed et al. (2025) (failure case: causality)
finding: Where the label depends on context, LLM agreement drops. Causality detection fell well below human level.
numbers: Causality: human-model 0.22 vs human-human 0.44; model-model 0.39 (under 0.5).
limits: Only top three models showed no answer bias.
agent_relevance: Use LLM coders on low-context labels only.

source: Xiao et al. (2023) Supporting Qualitative Analysis with LLMs: Combining Codebook with GPT-3 for Deductive Coding
finding: GPT-3 plus an expert codebook gives fair to substantial agreement with experts on deductive coding of curiosity-driven questions.
numbers: Cohen's kappa vs experts: Question complexity 0.61, Syntactic structure 0.38. Expert-expert: 0.88 and 0.90. Biggest gain from zero-shot to one-shot; few-shot no better than one-shot; codebook-centred prompt beat example-centred.
limits: Small, single dataset, GPT-3. Gap to expert-expert agreement remains.
agent_relevance: Prompt with the codebook plus one example; accept lower reliability than human pairs.

source: Kirsten et al. (2024) Decoding Complexity: Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding
finding: On three coding tasks of rising complexity, humans reached almost perfect agreement on two and substantial on the third. GPT-4 beat its predecessor on all tasks and was almost perfect on the easiest.
numbers: Humans: almost perfect on tasks A and B, substantial on C. GPT-4 almost perfect on Task A in all settings.
limits: Short paper. I read the intro and the start of the results only.
agent_relevance: Complexity of the codebook drives LLM-human agreement more than model choice.

source: Ernst, Treude (2026) GenAI Is No Silver Bullet for Qualitative Research in Software Engineering
finding: Scan of SE and HCI venues shows little GenAI use in coding. Reviews emerging evidence and warns that success on narrow deductive tasks does not extend to interpretive methods.
numbers: GenAI for coding reported in 7 of 209 screened CSCW papers (3%), 0 of 25 ICSE, 0 of 16 CHASE. Shah et al: kappa >0.7 as second annotator for user stories; zero-shot poor.
quote: Such claims are overgeneralizing from narrow successes.
limits: Small scan of three venues.
agent_relevance: Method note: LLMs can double-code defined labels; interpretation stays with humans.

source: Montes et al. as summarised by Ernst and Treude (2026)
finding: Reflexive thematic analysis of interview transcripts, human codes versus prompted GenAI codes, blinded.
numbers: 61% slight preference for GenAI codes; GenAI themes less aware of latent interpretations.
limits: Secondary source only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Preference for fluent codes can hide shallow themes.

source: Sallou, Durieux, Panichella (2024) Breaking the Silence: Threats of Using LLMs in Software Engineering
finding: Names three validity threats for LLM research: closed models that change, data leakage between pre-training and benchmarks, and poor reproducibility. Example: ChatGPT knows Defects4J bugs.
numbers: Illustrated with test generation; no large-sample numbers.
limits: Position paper, few numbers.
agent_relevance: Any benchmark result for our agent needs leakage and version checks.

source: Baltes et al. (2026) Guidelines for Empirical Studies in SE involving LLMs
finding: 22 researchers set a taxonomy of seven study types and eight guidelines (declare usage, report model version and config, document prompts, and more).
numbers: Angermeir et al (cited): of 85 LLM-centric ICSE/ASE 2024 papers, 18 used OpenAI models with artifacts; only 5 were runnable and none fully reproduced. Evertz et al (cited): pitfalls in all 72 papers; 15.7% of pitfalls discussed.
limits: Guidelines, not an experiment. Numbers are as cited by the guideline paper.
agent_relevance: Adopt these reporting rules for our own agent experiments.

source: Gerosa, Trinkenreich, Steinmacher, Sarma (2023) Can AI Serve as a Substitute for Human Subjects in SE Research?
finding: Vision paper proposing persona-based interviews, multi-persona focus groups and mega-persona surveys with LLMs for SE qualitative research.
numbers: No empirical numbers; sets agenda.
limits: Vision paper. I read the abstract only.
agent_relevance: Candidate method list; each needs the validity checks above.

source: Steinmacher et al. (2024) Can ChatGPT Emulate Humans in Software Engineering Surveys? ESEM 2024
finding: Replicated surveys published at SE venues 2019-2023 with a ChatGPT mega-persona. Some replicated; others were no better than a random baseline.
numbers: No per-survey numbers retrieved.
limits: Only a summary page was read, not the paper.
agent_relevance: SE survey replication by LLM is hit and miss.

source: Lin (2024) Six Fallacies in Substituting LLMs for Human Participants
finding: Lists six fallacies, including treating the LLM as an average human and treating alignment as explanation. Separates functional equivalence from mechanistic equivalence.
numbers: Conceptual paper.
limits: I read only the abstract.
agent_relevance: Argues for human evidence in any claim about process.
